## Part II - Point Estimation

### Chapter 4 - Frequentist Point Estimation

<details class="essential-points">
<summary> Assessment Focus </summary>


</details>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-statistic-estimator">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
<span class="xref-no-num">[Understand @sec-freq-point-estimate]</span> the distinction between a **statistic** and an **estimator**.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-statistic-estimator" hidden>

- A **statistic** is any quantity computed from data.  
  - When computed from random variables $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, it is **random**.  
  - When computed from observed values $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, it becomes **non-random**.
- An **estimator** $\hat{\theta}(\underline{X})$ is a statistic specifically designed to approximate a parameter $\theta$.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-estimator-estimate">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
<span class="xref-no-num">[Understand @sec-estimators-vs-estimates]</span> the difference between an **estimator** and an **estimate**.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-estimator-estimate" hidden>

- An **estimator** $\hat{\theta}(\underline{X})$ is a function of the **random sample** and is therefore **random**.
- An **estimate** $\hat{\theta}(\underline{x})$ is the numerical value obtained after plugging in the **observed data**, and is therefore **non-random**.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-sample-mean-var">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Be able to recall and use the definitions of the <span class="xref-no-num">[sample mean @def-sample-mean]</span> and the <span class="xref-no-num">[sample variance @def-sample-variance]</span>.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-sample-mean-var" hidden>

The <span class="xref-no-num">[sample mean @def-sample-mean]</span> is defined as
$$
\bar{X} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i.
$$
The <span class="xref-no-num">[sample variance @def-sample-variance]</span> is defined as
$$
S^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})^2.
$$

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-sampling-distribution">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Understand the concept of the <span class="xref-no-num">[sampling distribution @def-sampling-distribution]</span> of an estimator $\hat{\theta}$.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-sampling-distribution" hidden>

The <span class="xref-no-num">[sampling distribution @def-sampling-distribution]</span> of an estimator $\hat{\theta}$ is the probability distribution of $\hat{\theta}(\underline{X})$ when the data are repeatedly sampled from the model.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-normal-sample-mean">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Be able to <span class="xref-no-num">[recall @prp-normal-sample-mean]</span> and <span class="xref-no-num">[prove @prf-normal-sample-mean]</span> the sampling distribution of the sample mean for i.i.d. normal data.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-normal-sample-mean" hidden>

We use three key facts about the normal distribution:

1. The **sum** of normally distributed random variables is also normally distributed.  
2. Multiplying a normal random variable by a constant $c$ yields another normal random variable.  
3. A normal distribution is completely determined by its **mean** and **variance**.

Now consider i.i.d. normal data
$$
X_1,\ldots, X_n \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2).
$$

The sample mean
$$
\bar{X} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i
$$
is therefore also normally distributed. To determine its distribution, we compute its mean and variance:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{E}[\bar{X}]
  &= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathrm{E}[X_i]
   = \frac{n\mu}{n}
   = \mu, \\[6pt]
\mathrm{Var}(\bar{X})
  &= \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathrm{Var}(X_i)
   = \frac{n\sigma^2}{n^2}
   = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,
$$
\bar{X} \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(\mu,\, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
$$

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-bias-var-se-mse">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Be able to recall the definitions of, and compute, the <span class="xref-no-num">[bias @def-bias]</span>, <span class="xref-no-num">[variance @def-variance]</span>, <span class="xref-no-num">[standard error @def-se]</span> and <span class="xref-no-num">[mean-squared error (MSE) @def-mse]</span> of a given estimator.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-bias-var-se-mse" hidden>

1. <span class="xref-no-num">[Bias @def-bias]</span>: The *bias* of an estimator $\hat{\theta}$ of $\theta$ is
    $$
    \mathrm{Bias}(\hat{\theta}) = \mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}] - \theta.
    $$  
2. <span class="xref-no-num">[Variance @def-variance]</span>: The *variance* of an estimator $\hat{\theta}$ of $\theta$ is the **usual variance**:
    $$
    \mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}) = \mathrm{E}[(\hat{\theta} - \mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}])^2] = \mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}^2] - \mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}]^2.
    $$  
3. <span class="xref-no-num">[Standard error @def-se]</span>: The *standard error* of an estimator $\hat{\theta}$ of $\theta$ is the *standard deviation* of the estimator:
    $$
    \mathrm{S.E.}(\hat{\theta}) = \sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta})}.
    $$
4. <span class="xref-no-num">[Mean-squared error (MSE) @def-mse]</span>: The *mean-squared error* of an estimator $\hat{\theta}$ of $\theta$ is
    $$
    \mathrm{MSE}(\hat{\theta})=\mathrm{E}\!\big[(\hat{\theta}-\theta)^2\big].
    $$
  **Note:** When computing the MSE, always use the <span class="xref-no-num">[Bias–Variance decomposition @prp-mse-bias-variance]</span>:
  $$
  \mathrm{MSE}(\hat{\theta}) = \mathrm{Bias}(\hat{\theta})^2+\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}).
  $$ 

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-mse-bias-variance">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Be able to <span class="xref-no-num">[prove @prf-mse-bias-variance]</span> the <span class="xref-no-num">[Bias–Variance decomposition @prp-mse-bias-variance]</span> of the mean-squared error.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-mse-bias-variance" hidden>

There are two different approaches you could consider in proving @prp-mse-bias-variance.

--- 

**Approach 1:**

Start from the definition:

$$
\mathrm{MSE}(\hat{\theta})=\mathrm{E}\!\big[(\hat{\theta}-\theta)^2\big].
$$

**Step 1 (add–and–subtract the mean).** Let $m=\mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}]$. Then

$$
\hat{\theta}-\theta
=\big(\hat{\theta}-m\big)+\big(m-\theta\big).
$$

**Step 2 (expand the square).**

$$
(\hat{\theta}-\theta)^2
=\big(\hat{\theta}-m\big)^2
+2\big(\hat{\theta}-m\big)\big(m-\theta\big)
+\big(m-\theta\big)^2.
$$

**Step 3 (take expectations; use linearity).**

$$
\mathrm{E}\!\big[(\hat{\theta}-\theta)^2\big]
=\underbrace{\mathrm{E}\!\big[(\hat{\theta}-m)\!^2\big]}_{\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta})}
+2\,(m-\theta)\,\underbrace{\mathrm{E}\!\big[\hat{\theta}-m\big]}_{=\,0}
+\underbrace{(m-\theta)^2}_{\mathrm{Bias}(\hat{\theta})^2}.
$$

The middle term vanishes because $\mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}-m]=\mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}]-m=0$. Hence

$$
\mathrm{MSE}(\hat{\theta})
=\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta})+\big(\mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}]-\theta\big)^2
=\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta})+\mathrm{Bias}(\hat{\theta})^2.
$$

--- 

**Approach 2 (simpler):** 

Using the facts that
$$
\begin{align*}
    \mathrm{Bias}(\hat{\theta})^2 &= (\mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}] - \theta)^2 = \mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}]^2 - 2\theta \, \mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}] + \theta^2 \\
    \mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}) &= \mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}^2] - \mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}]^2,
\end{align*}
$$
we have
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{MSE}(\hat{\theta}) &= \mathrm{E}\big[(\hat{\theta} - \theta)^2\big] \\
&= \mathrm{E}\big[\hat{\theta}^2 - 2\,\theta \, \hat{\theta} + \theta^2\big] \\
&= \mathrm{E}\big[\hat{\theta}^2 \big] -2\theta \mathrm{E}\big[\hat{\theta} \big] + \theta^2 \\ 
&= \underbrace{\mathrm{E}\big[\hat{\theta}^2 \big] - \mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}]^2}_{=\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta})} + \underbrace{\mathrm{E}[\hat{\theta}]^2-2\theta \mathrm{E}\big[\hat{\theta} \big] + \theta^2}_{=\mathrm{Bias}(\hat{\theta})^2} \\
&= \mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}) + \mathrm{Bias}(\hat{\theta})^2.
\end{align*}
$$

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-asymptotic">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Understand the meaning of <span class="xref-no-num">[asymptotic @imp-term-asymptotic]</span> in statistics.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-asymptotic" hidden>

 An asymptotic result describes the behaviour of an estimator or statistic as the sample size $n$ (in data $X_1,\ldots,X_n$) becomes **very large**.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-clt">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Be able to recall and understand the <span class="xref-no-num">[Central Limit Theorem @thm-clt]</span>.  
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-clt" hidden>

The CLT tells us that for i.i.d. observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ from **any distribution** with finite variance $\sigma^2 < \infty$, the **sample mean** becomes approximately normal as $n$ grows:
$$
\bar{X} \;\overset{\text{approx.}}{\sim}\;
\mathcal{N}\!\left(\mu,\, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
$$

This **exam requires only this practical form** of the CLT - no proofs or more general statements are needed.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-asymp-unbiased-consistent">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Be able to recall the definitions of <span class="xref-no-num">[asymptotic unbiasedness @def-asymptotic-unbiasedness]</span> and <span class="xref-no-num">[consistency @def-consistency]</span>.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-asymp-unbiased-consistent" hidden>

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-consistency-proof">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Be able to show that an estimator is <span class="xref-no-num">[consistent @def-consistency]</span>
  using the <span class="xref-no-num">[sufficient conditions @prp-sufficient-consistency]</span>.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-consistency-proof" hidden>

Consider an estimator $\hat{\theta}_n$ of a parameter $\theta$, based on a sample of size $n$. A **consistent estimator** must satisfy:

1. **Asymptotic unbiasedness:**
    $$
    \mathrm{Bias}(\hat{\theta}_n) \;\longrightarrow \; 0 \qquad \text{as } n \to \infty,
    $$

2. **Vanishing variance:**
    $$
    \mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}_n) \;\longrightarrow\; 0 \qquad \text{as } n \to \infty.
    $$

Together, these conditions imply that $\hat{\theta}_n$ is a **consistent estimator**.

**Note:** For exam purposes, you can *always* use these sufficient conditions to prove consistency: check the bias tends to $0$ and the variance tends to $0$ as $n$ grows.

</div>
</div>

### Chapter 5 - Likelihood

<details class="essential-points">
<summary> Assessment Focus </summary>

- The **vast majority** of examinable material involves computing <span class="xref-no-num">[likelihood functions @def-likelihood]</span>. It is therefore **essential** that you are fully confident in computing likelihoods across a range of statistical models.

</details>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-likelihood-def">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Understand the **definition** of the <span class="xref-no-num">[likelihood function @def-likelihood]</span>.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-likelihood-def" hidden>

Given a statistical model  
$$
X_1,\ldots,X_n \sim \mathrm{Distribution}(\theta),
$$
the **joint density (or PMF)** of the observed data $\underline{x}$, viewed as a function of the parameter $\theta$, is the likelihood:
$$
L(\theta;\,\underline{x}) = f(\underline{x}\mid\theta).
$$
The data are treated as fixed, and the likelihood expresses how plausible different values of $\theta$ are in light of those observations.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-likelihood-factorisation">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
<span class="xref-no-num">[Understand @sec-likelihood-dependence]</span> how the likelihood function factorises under different assumptions about the data.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-likelihood-factorisation" hidden>

There are **three cases**:

1. **Independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.):** If the data satisfy
   $$
   X_1,\ldots,X_n \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathrm{Distribution}(\theta),
   $$
   then each observation has the *same* density (or PMF) $f(x_i \mid \theta)$, and independence gives the factorisation
   $$
   L(\theta;\underline{x}) = f(\underline{x}\mid\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i \mid \theta).
   $$

2. **Independent but not identically distributed:** If the data are independent but may follow different distributions, then
   $$
   f(\underline{x}\mid\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f_{X_i}(x_i \mid \theta),
   $$
   where each $f_{X_i}(x_i \mid \theta)$ is the density (or PMF) for the observation $X_i$.

3. **Dependent data:** The general case, in which the $X_i$ are *not* independent, is **not examinable** in this module.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-compute-likelihood">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Be able to <span class="xref-no-num">[compute @sec-computing-likelihoods]</span> likelihood functions for general statistical models, under both i.i.d. assumptions and the more general case of independent (but not necessarily identically distributed) data.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-compute-likelihood" hidden>

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-mle-def">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Be able to recall and understand the <span class="xref-no-num">[definition @def-mle]</span> of the **Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE)**. In particular, understand the meaning of <span class="xref-no-num">[the argmax notation @imp-term-argmax-max]</span> in the definition.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-mle-def" hidden>

The <span class="xref-no-num">[definition @def-mle]</span> of the Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE) is
$$
\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}
   = \argmax_{\theta \in \Theta} \, L(\theta;\,\underline{X}),
$$
where $\Theta$ denotes the **parameter space** (the set of all permissible values of $\theta$).

- The notation **argmax** means *"the value of $\theta$ that maximises the function"*.  
- In other words, $\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}$ is the choice of $\theta$ that makes the observed data **most likely** under the model.

</div>
</div>


<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-compute-mle">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Be able to compute <span class="xref-no-num">[univariate MLEs @sec-computing-univariate-mles]</span>.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-compute-mle" hidden>

**General Procedure**

1. **Write down the likelihood**  
   $$L(\theta; \underline{x}) = f(\underline{x} \mid \theta).$$

2. **Compute the log-likelihood**  
   $$\ell(\theta; \underline{x}) = \log L(\theta; \underline{x}).$$

3. **Differentiate the log-likelihood**  
   Compute  
   $$
   \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta}\,\ell(\theta;\underline{x}).
   $$

4. **Set the derivative equal to zero and solve**  
   Find all solutions to  
   $$
   \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta}\,\ell(\theta;\underline{x}) = 0.
   $$

---

**Notes:**

- Unless the question explicitly states otherwise, you do **not** need to check whether the solution corresponds to a maximum.  
  For this module, you may assume any solution you find is the global maximiser.

- Computing **multivariate MLEs** is *not examinable*.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-fisher-info">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Be able to <span class="xref-no-num">[compute @imp-compute-fisher-info]</span> and recall the <span class="xref-no-num">[definition of Fisher information @def-fisher-information]</span>. 
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-fisher-info" hidden>

There are two versions to distinguish:

- **Fisher information for a single observation**
  $$
  \mathcal{I}_1(\theta)
    = -\,\mathrm{E}\!\left[
        \frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}
        \log f(X \mid \theta)
      \right].
  $$

- **Fisher information for the whole sample**
  $$
  \mathcal{I}_n(\theta)
    = -\,\mathrm{E}\!\left[
        \frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}
        \ell(\theta;\underline{X})
      \right],
  $$
  where $\ell(\theta;\underline{X})$ is the log-likelihood of all $n$ observations.

---

**Note:** In this module, you will almost always be asked to compute the **Fisher information for the whole sample**. For consistency and simplicity, we recommend using **Approach 1** described <span class="xref-no-num">[here @imp-compute-fisher-info]</span>.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-crlb">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Be able to recall the <span class="xref-no-num">[Cramér–Rao Lower Bound @thm-crlb]</span>.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-crlb" hidden>

- The Cramér–Rao inequality states that for **any unbiased estimator** $\hat{\theta}$ of a parameter $\theta$,
  $$
  \mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}) \;\ge\; \mathcal{I}_n(\theta)^{-1},
  $$
  where $\mathcal{I}_n(\theta)^{-1}$ is the **Cramér–Rao Lower Bound (CRLB)**.

- This result is extremely important because, for unbiased estimators,
  $$
  \mathrm{MSE}(\hat{\theta}) = \mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}).
  $$
  So, the CRLB provides a theoretical minimum: it tells us the best possible performance an unbiased estimator can achieve.

- If an unbiased estimator **achieves** the CRLB, it is called <span class="xref-no-num">[efficient @def-efficiency]</span>, meaning no other unbiased estimator has smaller variance.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-efficiency">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Be able to show whether a given estimator is <span class="xref-no-num">[efficient @def-efficiency]</span>.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-efficiency" hidden>

An <span class="xref-no-num">[efficient @def-efficiency]</span> estimator is an unbiased estimator whose variance is equal to the <span class="xref-no-num">[Cramér–Rao Lower Bound @thm-crlb]</span>. That is, an estimator $\hat{\theta}$ of $\theta$ such that
$$
\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}) =  \mathcal{I}_n(\theta)^{-1},
$$
and $\mathrm{Bias}(\hat{\theta}) = 0$.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-asymp-mle">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Be able to recall and compute the <span class="xref-no-num">[asymptotic sampling distribution of the MLE @def-asymp-mle-approx]</span>.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-asymp-mle" hidden>

This result states that for data  
$$
X_1,\ldots,X_n \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathrm{Distribution}(\theta),
$$
from **any model**, the <span class="xref-no-num">[maximum likelihood estimator @def-mle]</span> satisfies
$$
\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}
\;\overset{\text{approx.}}{\sim}\;
\mathcal{N}\!\left(
    \theta,\;
    \mathcal{I}_n \big(\theta \big)^{-1}
\right),
\qquad \text{for large } n.
$$

---

**Notes:** 

- In practice, we usually replace the unknown parameter $\theta$ with its estimate $\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}$ inside the Fisher information. 
- So, for the exam, it is sufficient to remember the **plug-in form** $\mathcal{I}_n\big(\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}\big)$. 
- This **plug-in form** $\mathcal{I}_n\big(\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}\big)$, is called the <span class="xref-no-num">[observed Fisher information @def-observed-fisher]</span>.

</div>
</div>

### Chapter 6 - Bayesian Inference

<details class="essential-points">
<summary> Assessment Focus </summary>

1. You will primarily be assessed on your ability to:
   1. **Compute posterior distributions**, substitute observed data, and interpret the resulting inference.  
   2. **Assess whether a prior distribution is consistent** with stated prior beliefs.  
   3. **Interpret and compare** Bayesian and Frequentist approaches to inference.  
   4. **Compute Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) estimators.**  
   5. **Obtain asymptotic posteriors** using large-sample approximations.

2. Among all posterior calculations in the course, the most **algebraically involved** is <span class="xref-no-num">[this @q-normal-normal]</span> question, where  
   $$
   X_i \mid \mu \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \gamma), \qquad \mu \sim \mathcal{N}(m, v).
   $$
   Be prepared to work through this derivation carefully.

</details>


<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-bayes-approach">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
<span class="xref-no-num">[Understand @sec-intro-bayes-approach]</span> how the **Bayesian** approach differs from the **Frequentist** approach.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-bayes-approach" hidden>

In the **Bayesian** framework, the parameter $\theta$ is treated as a **random variable**. 

  - Its randomness represents our **uncertainty** about the true value of $\theta$.

In contrast, the **Frequentist** approach treats $\theta$ as a **fixed but unknown constant**.  

  - All randomness comes solely from the data, not from the parameter.

</div>
</div>


<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-bayes-procedure">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
<span class="xref-no-num">[Understand @sec-bayes-inference-procedure]</span> the **Bayesian** inference procedure:
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-bayes-procedure" hidden>

Bayesian inference is built around three core components:

- **Prior:** Describes our beliefs about the parameter $\theta$ *before* seeing any data. Its PDF is written as
  $$
  \pi(\theta).
  $$

- **Likelihood:** Comes from specifying a statistical model  
  $$
  X_i \mid \theta \sim \mathrm{Distribution}(\theta).
  $$  
  This determines the joint density of the observed data,  
  $$
  f(\underline{x} \mid \theta),
  $$  
  which tells us how plausible the data are *for each possible value* of $\theta$.

- **Posterior:** Updates the prior using the information in the data. It summarises our **revised beliefs** about $\theta$ after observing $\underline{x}$, and its PDF is written as
  $$
  \pi(\theta \mid \underline{x}).
  $$  
  This is the quantity from which all Bayesian estimates, intervals, and predictions are derived.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-bayes-theorem-density">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Be able to <span class="xref-no-num">[prove @prf-bayes]</span> and recall <span class="xref-no-num">[Bayes theorem for densities @thm-bayes-density]</span> and understand how this yields the **posterior density**:
$$
\pi(\theta \mid \underline{x}) = \frac{\pi(\theta) \, f(\underline{x}\mid \theta)}{f(\underline{x})}.
$$
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-bayes-theorem-density" hidden>

To obtain the posterior, we simply apply Bayes’ theorem to the parameter $\theta$ and the observed data $\underline{x}$.  

The usual density form in @thm-bayes-density is
$$
f(x \mid y) = \frac{f(y \mid x)\,f(x)}{f(y)}.
$$
It is relabelled as follows:

- **Parameter:** $x = \theta$
- **Data:** $y = \underline{x}$
- **Prior:** $f(x) = \pi(\theta)$
- **Likelihood:** $f(y \mid x) = f(\underline{x} \mid \theta)$
- **Posterior:** $f(x \mid y) = \pi(\theta \mid \underline{x})$

Substituting these into Bayes’ theorem gives:
$$
\pi(\theta \mid \underline{x})
= \frac{\pi(\theta)\,f(\underline{x}\mid \theta)}
       {f(\underline{x})},
$$
where the denominator
$$
f(\underline{x}) = \int \pi(\theta)\,f(\underline{x}\mid \theta)\,d\theta
$$
acts only as a **normalising constant**, ensuring the posterior integrates to $1$.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-proportionality">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Understand that we **do not need to compute** the normalisation constant $f(\underline{x})$. It is **sufficient** to know the posterior up to a <span class="xref-no-num">[constant of proportionality @imp-bayes-proportionality]</span>.
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-proportionality" hidden>

When computing posterior distributions in Bayesian inference, **always use**

$$
\pi(\theta \mid \underline{x}) \propto \pi(\theta) \, f(\underline{x}\mid \theta).
$$
and the approach outlined <span class="xref-no-num">[here @imp-compute-posterior]</span>.

</div>
</div>

<div class="revision-entry">
<div class="revision-header" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="rev-conjugacy">
<span class="toggle-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="revision-topic">
Be able to compute the distribution of the posterior $\pi(\theta \mid \underline{x})$ using the idea of <span class="xref-no-num">[conjugacy @def-conjugacy]</span>. 
</span>
</div>

<div class="revision-content" id="rev-conjugacy" hidden>

The steps to compute a posterior can be found <span class="xref-no-num">[here @imp-compute-posterior]</span>.

</div>
</div>
